## How to specify an industrial computer
Four questions that shape the platform, the I/O set and the mechanical design.

### 1. Software first
List the operating system, runtime, drivers and CPU class your application actually needs.

### 2. I/O and expansion
Count the serial ports, LAN ports, USB devices and expansion slots the installation requires.

### 3. Environment
Record ambient temperature, dust, vibration, power input range and available mounting space.

### 4. Lifecycle
Agree the supply period, revision control and what happens when a component reaches end of life.

# OEM/ODM Custom Kiosk Enclosure & Integration | Xinyuehong

URL: https://xinyuehongtech.com/customization/


# OEM & ODM Self-Service Kiosk Projects
Two routes to a self-service terminal that carries your own brand: adapt one of our existing kiosk platforms, or develop a new enclosure and hardware set around your brief. Both start with a written specification.

## OEM or ODM: which route fits
The difference is how much of the product already exists.

### OEM: your brand on a proven platform
Start from an existing kiosk platform and adjust screen size, colour, logo, peripherals and the software image. Faster to quote and to deliver because the mechanics and thermal design already work.

### ODM: build the product around your brief
Where no existing cabinet meets the size, mounting or function you need, the enclosure, mechanical layout and peripheral set are developed together. More preparation, far more freedom.

## What can be customised
Feasibility and exact scope are confirmed during the specification review, before anything is quoted as final.

### Cabinet & appearance
Size, material, mounting, cabinet colour, logo placement and mechanical design requirements.

### Touchscreen & computing
Display orientation, screen size, PC platform, operating system and connectivity selection.

### Peripheral integration
Scanner, thermal printer, camera, NFC/RFID reader and compatible payment device planning.

### Software & interfaces
Application fit, SDK/API requirements, ports, drivers and third-party back-end integration review.

### Branding & user experience
Custom front graphics, user touch points, installation guidance and service access design.

### Validation & rollout
Prototype review, functional testing, target-market requirements and acceptance checkpoints.

## From requirement to a finished terminal
Seven stages, each ending with something you can approve in writing before the next one starts.

### Requirement
Application, target market, module list, volume, certification needs and target date written into one brief.

### Feasibility & budget
OEM or ODM route chosen; standard parts and changed parts separated, then quoted line by line.

### Enclosure design
3D structure, module layout, cable routing, colour and artwork agreed on drawing.

### Prototype
Sample built; Windows, Android or Linux image loaded and every embedded module driven by its driver or SDK.

### Validation
Sample reviewed against your software, interfaces tested, and a closed change list signed off.

### Pilot run
Process documents, ageing test and outgoing inspection criteria fixed before volume work begins.

### Production & shipping
Batch build, unit-by-unit inspection, packing and shipping documents; repeat orders keyed to the same specification.
Stages 1–2 define the product, 3–5 build and prove it, 6–7 repeat it. No volume production starts before the sample and its interfaces are approved.

## What happens at each stage
The detail behind the diagram.

### 1. Send the brief
Share the application, target country, reference images if you have them, required peripherals, estimated volume and target schedule.

### 2. Route and budget
We recommend OEM or ODM, list the parts that stay standard and the ones that change, and quote on that basis.

### 3. Specification and sample
Drawings, finishes, logos and interfaces are written down. Where it pays off, build or review a sample before volume work.

### 4. Volume and repeat orders
Agree the acceptance criteria, what stays identical between batches, and how later changes are approved.

# About Us | Self-Service Kiosk Manufacturer | Xinyuehong

# About Xinyuehong
Xinyuehong is a Shenzhen-based team working on self-service kiosk terminals and the industrial computers that run them. This page explains how projects are handled and what to prepare before you write to us.

## A hardware partner for self-service work
Xinyuehong works on customer-facing self-service hardware: ordering terminals, payment and check-in kiosks, ticketing machines, information points, and the fanless computers, boards, panel PCs and gateways that sit inside them.
Most conversations start with a problem rather than a product: a queue that grows too long, a counter that cannot stay staffed, or a task that employees repeat hundreds of times a day. We work backwards from that task to decide screen size, enclosure style, peripheral set and computing platform.
Every project is built to a written specification. Interfaces, finishes, quantities, power requirements and delivery expectations are confirmed on both sides before production starts, so everyone knows what the finished unit is supposed to be.

## What we work on
Four areas that decide whether a terminal survives contact with real users.

### Requirement review
Your application flow, software stack and venue constraints are reviewed first, and anything that will not work is flagged before a quotation is issued.

### Enclosure design
Cabinet form factor, material, finish, colour, logo treatment, service access and cable routing are considered as one mechanical package.

### Peripheral integration
Printers, scanners, cameras, card readers and payment-device mounting are planned with the enclosure instead of being added afterwards.

### Platform selection
Fanless box PCs, boards, panel PCs and gateways are matched to the operating system, I/O count and installation environment.

## Inside the factory
The same floor that builds prototypes builds production batches - assembly, sheet metal, coating and burn-in testing are all in-house.

## How a project runs
The same four stages whether you order a single unit or a repeat batch.

### 1. Send the brief
Describe the application, estimated quantity, target environment and any software that must run on the unit.

### 2. Confirm the specification
Screens, peripherals, interfaces, finishes, power and mounting are written down and agreed by both sides.

### 3. Review before volume
Where a project justifies it, drawings or a sample unit are evaluated before repeated production.

### 4. Production and repeat orders
Agree in advance which parts stay stable across batches and how later changes are handled.

## Questions we are asked first

# Airport Self Check-in Kiosks & Bag Tag Printing | Xinyuehong

URL: https://xinyuehongtech.com/industries/airport-aviation/


# Airport Self Check-in Kiosks & Bag Tag Printing
A departures hall is a throughput problem measured in seconds per passenger. The constraint is rarely the screen; it is the document check, the boarding pass, and the bag tag — three different printers and readers in one footprint, working under a queue that forms three hours before departure.

## Where the departures queue actually forms
Check-in opens two to three hours before departure and peaks in a 40-minute window. A single desk handles roughly one passenger every 90 seconds when documents are in order; the queue grows when a passport needs a second look or a bag exceeds the allowance. A self-service unit earns its place by taking the passengers whose documents are clean and whose bag can be self-tagged.
The second pressure point is the transfer passenger. They arrive with a boarding pass already issued, need no bag tag, and only want a seat change or a reprint. Sending them to the same queue as a full check-in wastes the desk's capacity; a kiosk that can reprint and re-seat absorbs them in under a minute.
The third is language. An international airport may need six or eight languages on the same screen, and the document prompts have to be unambiguous in all of them. That is a layout decision — the longest translated string sets the button width — not a translation exercise added at the end.

## Terminals for check-in and bag tagging
Cabinets that carry document readers, a boarding pass printer and a bag tag printer in one footprint.
32-inch QHD portrait screen with passport MRZ reader option, camera bar, card readers and an 80 mm printer in the side column.
Vertical touchscreen with a thermal printer, ticket outlet and deck scanner, for boarding pass and receipt printing.
ID document reader with MRZ support, plus social-security, bank and contactless card readers for identity-heavy flows.

## What an airport specification has to settle

### Passport and visa capture
MRZ reading is the baseline; chip reading and visa pages depend on the reader module and on what the airline's DCS accepts. The reader set is fixed before the deck is drawn.

### ATB or A4
ATB stock needs a dedicated printer and a defined paper path; A4 is cheaper but slower per passenger. Both can be fitted, and the choice follows the airline's boarding process.

### IATA tag stock
Bag tag printing needs a printer module sized for the tag stock and a collection point at standing height. The printer, not the screen, is usually the throughput limit.

### CUSS and DCS
Airport common-use deployments normally require a CUSS-certified application approved by the airport authority. The kiosk supplies the peripheral layer; the certification lives with the application provider.

### Seconds per passenger
Document read, seat confirmation, two print jobs. If the bag tag and boarding pass come out of the same slot, the queue stalls; two outlets keep it moving.

### Restock and jams
Tag stock, boarding pass stock and receipt paper are three consumables with three access points. All of them have to be replaceable by airport staff during a turnaround.

## Procurement checklist
- The DCS or check-in platform, and whether a CUSS-certified application is mandatory at the airport
- Document types accepted: passport MRZ, chip, national ID, visa
- Boarding pass format (ATB stock or A4) and bag tag stock specification
- Bag tag and boarding pass outlet positions, and whether one slot or two
- Languages required, and the longest translated string
- Hall layout: power, network, floor fixing, and the queue geometry around the unit
- Consumable restock procedure and who performs it
- Pilot scope: one terminal bank, measured on passengers processed per hour and intervention rate
Airport projects move fastest when the application provider is already CUSS-certified and the peripheral list is fixed. We can supply reference details of self check-in units delivered for airport projects on request.

## Questions we are asked first
Can the kiosk print bag tags?
Does the kiosk support CUSS?
Can it print both a boarding pass and a bag tag?
Which documents can it read?
How many passengers per hour can one unit handle?
Can the interface run in several languages?

# Bank Self-Service Kiosks & Branch Terminals | Xinyuehong

URL: https://xinyuehongtech.com/industries/banking/


# Bank & Branch Self-Service Kiosks
Branch self-service is a privacy problem before it is a hardware problem. Every design decision — screen recess, PIN pad placement, queue direction, cabinet depth — follows from the fact that a customer is entering a PIN in public.

## Three ways banks deploy these terminals
The common failure across all three is specifying the cabinet before the payment device. A PIN pad that is not yet approved, or a card reader that arrives with a different bezel, forces a re-cut fascia — the most expensive kind of change in a small programme.

## Terminals for branch self-service
Four cabinets covering enquiry, card issue, queue management and cash.
27-inch branch terminal with an encrypting PIN pad and privacy hood, swipe, chip and contactless readers, QR scanner and 80 mm printer.
ATM-style cabinet with a recessed anti-peep screen, separate encrypting keypad, EMV reader and an optional cash acceptor behind the secure fascia.
Brushed stainless cabinet with a 2560 × 1440 portrait screen for account, card and document workflows that need more than a tile menu.
Queue-ticket terminal for busy branches, with a printed ticket, a QR scanner at the deck and an 80 mm printer outlet.

## Specification points that decide the project

### The PIN pad is never integrated
An encrypting PIN pad is a separately certified device. It sits in its own module bay with a privacy hood, and it can be swapped for a bank-qualified model without re-drawing the cabinet.

### Recess, hood, orientation
A portrait screen with a recessed face and a hooded keypad lets the next customer stand behind the user's shoulder without seeing the screen. Queue direction is part of the drawing.

### Per market, per device
Payment certification follows the device and the acquirer, not the cabinet. A build that is compliant in one market is not automatically compliant in another, so the destination country belongs in the enquiry.

### Cash changes the cabinet
A cash acceptor or recycler needs depth, a secure fascia and a service procedure. Card-only builds are smaller, cheaper and faster to certify; cash should be a deliberate choice.

### Bolt-down and alarm-ready
For unsupervised lobbies, the plinth has a bolt-down option and the cabinet carries mounting points for an alarm contact or security seal supplied by your contractor.

### Who opens it, and how
Paper and module access should be a front operation that branch staff can perform. If a service visit is needed every time the printer runs out, the unit will sit empty instead.

## Procurement checklist
- The PIN pad model and its approval status in the target market
- The payment device model, bezel drawing and mounting footprint
- Which services the terminal will offer, in the order the customer meets them
- Whether the site is supervised, or open to the public overnight
- Cash handling: none, acceptor only, or acceptor plus recycler
- Queue layout, and the clear space in front of the screen
- Cleaning and first-line maintenance: who changes paper, who resets a jam
- Destination country, because it sets the certification path

## Questions we are asked first
Can we fit our own certified PIN pad instead of the supplied unit?
Is a card-only terminal cheaper and faster to deploy than a cash build?
How much space does the terminal need in front of it?
Can the kiosk print statements on A4 instead of a receipt slip?

# Ticketing & Entertainment Kiosks for Venues | Xinyuehong

URL: https://xinyuehongtech.com/industries/entertainment-ticketing/


# Ticketing & Entertainment Kiosks for Venues
A venue entrance has one hard deadline: the doors open at a fixed time and everyone arrives within twenty minutes. A ticket kiosk that issues or collects in under thirty seconds absorbs the pre-booked crowd, which is where the queue is longest and the staff are least useful.

## Buying and collecting are two different queues
Collection is the volume problem. Most visitors now arrive with a booking on their phone, so the machine's job is to scan a QR code and print a ticket, not to walk through a seat map. That is a fifteen-second transaction, and it fails if the scanner is slow or the printer outlet is placed where the ticket falls on the floor.
Purchase is the exception. It needs a seat map, a payment step and a slower interaction, and it should not be in the same queue as collection or it slows both. Venues with space for two cabinets usually dedicate one to collection and keep purchase to the box office; venues with one cabinet use a screen selection at the start.
The third constraint is the venue itself: a cinema lobby is warm, a stadium concourse is cold and crowded, and both are cleaned aggressively. The front face has to survive that, and the paper path has to be clearable by venue staff in under a minute.

## Terminals for venues
Collection, vending and queue management in cabinets sized for a lobby.
Separate issue and collection outlets with a QR scanner, so a pre-booked visitor does not queue behind a purchase.
Vertical touchscreen with thermal ticket printer, outlet and deck scanner for venues with a single queue.
Large portrait screen for seat maps and membership flows, with scanner and card reader on the deck.

## What a venue specification has to settle

### QR at the right height
The scanner has to read a phone screen at a comfortable angle, not force the visitor to hold the phone flat against a glass plate at waist height.

### Ticket stock
Thermal ticket stock with a dedicated outlet, or A4 where the venue issues full-page passes. The cutter rating matters more than the print speed at a 20-minute peak.

### Contactless first
Card and phone payment through a certified terminal mounted on the cabinet. Cash is usually the exception at venues and can be omitted to simplify the build.

### Seconds per visitor
Collection should complete in fifteen to twenty seconds. Two outlets — ticket and receipt — keep a family group from blocking the next person.

### Lobby or concourse
Cinema lobby and open concourse are different cases. Dust, temperature and cleaning chemicals all change the front face and the sealing.

### Ticketing platform
The kiosk prints what the platform returns. Seat maps, allocation and validation are application-level, and the interface is confirmed before the cabinet is drawn.

## Procurement checklist
- Split between collection and purchase, and how many cabinets for each
- Ticket stock: thermal roll, pre-printed stock, or A4
- Whether the scanner must read phone screens at full brightness
- Payment methods: contactless, chip, or none at collection
- Venue conditions: indoor lobby, covered concourse, outdoor queue
- Ticketing platform and who owns the integration
- Consumable restock and jam clearance by venue staff
- Peak window: how many visitors in how many minutes

## Questions we are asked first
Can one kiosk both sell and collect tickets?
What ticket stock does the printer take?
Will the scanner read a phone screen?
Do we need cash acceptance?
Can the kiosk work outdoors at a stadium?

# Government & Municipal Self-Service Kiosks | Xinyuehong

URL: https://xinyuehongtech.com/industries/government/


# Government & Municipal Self-Service Kiosks
A citizen service hall is a document-processing building with a queue attached. The kiosk that survives there is the one whose reader set matches the documents people actually bring, not the one with the largest screen.

## Document first, screen second
Most public-service transactions start with a document: a national ID, a social-security card, a residence permit, a passport, or a form the citizen has already filled in at home. The reader set therefore comes before the interface. A hall that reads second-generation ID cards needs a reader module for that card; a hall that handles passports needs an MRZ reader; a hall that takes payment needs a bank card reader as well.
The second characteristic of these halls is that the same cabinet is used by different agencies. A social-security counter, a records desk and a permits window may share the same unit, with different software. That is why the multi-reader cabinet matters more here than in any other sector: the module bank has to accept the union of what the agencies need, not the requirement of the first one to deploy.
The third is throughput. A citizen hall is measured in people per hour, and the constraint is usually the printing at the end of the transaction, not the touchscreen. A queue ticket printer, a certificate printer and a receipt printer are three different modules with three different duty cycles, and mixing them up is how a terminal becomes the new bottleneck.
Finally, accessibility is not optional in a public building. Screen height, reach distance, contrast, a keyboard for people who cannot use a touchscreen, and a clear route for wheelchair users are all drawing-stage decisions that are expensive to retrofit.

## Terminals for public service halls
Six cabinets covering citizen services, social security, immigration and queue management.
ID document reader with MRZ support, social-security and bank card readers, QR scanner and 80 mm printer on a 27-inch portrait screen.
23.8-inch working screen plus a 21.5-inch guidance screen for the queue, with a multi-slot national ID, social-security and bank card reader bank.
Reduced-depth cabinet for corridor placement, with a social-security card slot, ID scanner, compact keyboard and receipt printer.
32-inch working screen with an upper guidance display, a large cabinet and an optional A4 printer for permit application and collection.
Service island with four independent reader slots, a full-size keyboard and a guidance display, for lanes that handle mixed credential types.
Queue-ticket terminal for service halls, with a printed ticket, QR scanner and card reader at the deck.

## What public-sector specifications must settle

### The exact document list
MRZ reading, second-generation ID, residence permits and paper forms are different readers and different placement. The list is fixed before the deck is drawn.

### One cabinet, several services
If two or three agencies will use the unit, the reader bank is specified for the union of their needs, and the software decides which service is shown.

### Ticket, certificate, receipt
Queue tickets and receipts fit an 80 mm module. Certificates and A4 forms need a document printer, and that usually means the larger cabinet with front paper access.

### Height, reach, contrast
Public buildings have to serve people who cannot stand for long, cannot see small text or cannot use a touchscreen. Each of those changes the drawing rather than the software.

### More than one language
Bilingual or trilingual interfaces are normal in this sector. The screen layout has to accommodate longer strings without breaking the form fields below them.

### Who did what, when
Public transactions are audited. The terminal passes identity and transaction events to the agency system; the retention policy lives there, not in the cabinet.

## Procurement checklist
- The complete list of documents the terminal must read, with the document types named
- Which agencies will use the unit, and whether they share one software stack
- What is printed: queue ticket, receipt, certificate, or a multi-page form
- Accessibility requirements from the building standard, not from a supplier brochure
- Languages required on screen, and the longest string in each
- Where the unit stands: hall, corridor, counter line, or an outdoor checkpoint
- The agency system interface, and who supports it after handover
- Service model: who restocks paper, who clears a jam, who is called when a reader fails

## Questions we are asked first
Which identity documents can the terminals read?
Can one cabinet serve several agencies with different services?
Can the terminal print certificates, or only queue tickets?
How do we handle a unit that serves wheelchair users and standing adults?

# Hospital Self-Service Kiosks & Payment Terminals | Xinyuehong

URL: https://xinyuehongtech.com/industries/hospital/


# Hospital Self-Service Kiosks
An outpatient visit is not one transaction. It is registration, a queue number, a consultation fee, a test payment and a report collection, each at a different counter. A hospital kiosk project only works when the hardware is mapped to those steps first.

## Where the outpatient queue actually breaks
In most hospitals the first bottleneck is not the doctor, it is the registration window at 08:00. A patient who arrives without an appointment joins a queue to be registered, then a second queue to pay, then a third to collect a report. Each counter repeats the same identity check, and each handover is where the wait accumulates.
The second bottleneck appears after the consultation: the payment step. A patient who has just been told what tests they need is sent back to a cashier desk, which is often the busiest window in the building. Moving that payment next to the consultation area — or onto the ward — removes a queue without adding staff.
The third is the report. Radiology and laboratory results are printed at a counter that closes earlier than the wards, so a patient who finishes tests in the afternoon comes back the next morning for a piece of paper. A printing terminal that verifies identity and releases the document on demand removes that second visit entirely.
These three steps have different hardware requirements, which is why a single "hospital kiosk" rarely fits all of them. The guide below maps each step to a cabinet, and the cabinet to the modules that make it work.

## Terminals for each step of a visit
Reference builds from our range, chosen by the task rather than by the department.
Dual-screen unit for outpatient registration, appointment check-in and self-payment, with IC, ID and bank card readers, a retractable keyboard and an 80 mm receipt printer.
Corridor and lift-lobby payment point with an encrypting PIN pad, card readers and a receipt printer, for floors that cannot spare floor area.
A4 record and report printing released after an ID check, with front paper access and a collection slot at the bottom of the cabinet.
Insurance balance, claim status and card validation on a curved 27-inch portrait screen, with a document scanner under the display.
Registration plus physical card issue from a 100-card motorised hopper, for community clinics and health centres.
Braked-castor station for bedside payment and temporary screening points, with a second screen facing the patient.

## What a hospital specification has to include
Six items that cause most rework when they are decided late.

### Three identity routes
ID card, medical insurance card and a booking reference are three different reads. Decide which the registration flow accepts before the reader deck is drawn, not after the cabinet is built.

### Payment inside or beside
A certified third-party terminal is the usual route, mounted on the cabinet with its own approval. An integrated reader is possible where the acquirer and the hospital's finance team both accept it.

### Slip or A4
Queue tickets and receipts need an 80 mm thermal printer. Records, invoices and itemised bills need A4, which changes the cabinet and the paper access — usually to a front-loading design.

### Wipeable front face
Flat glass, stainless keycaps and a retractable keyboard are specified because the front face is cleaned between patients. Deep recesses and fabric surfaces are the parts infection-control teams reject.

### Height and reach
Seated patients, wheelchair users and elderly users set the screen height, the keyboard reach and whether a second lower screen is needed. This is fixed at the drawing stage with the hospital's accessibility standard The

### One cable, one policy
The kiosk needs a stable wired connection to the hospital system, and a maintenance window that does not clash with clinic hours. Remote update policy belongs in the project plan, not in the hardware order.

## Procurement checklist
What to have on paper before you ask for a quotation.
- The registration flow, written as steps, including which identity document is read at which step
- Which payments the terminal must take, and whether a certified third-party device is mandatory
- What is printed at each terminal: queue slip, receipt, invoice or full record
- Where each unit stands: outpatient hall, corridor, ward, lift lobby, or a mobile station
- Who uses it: standing adults only, or also seated and wheelchair users
- The hospital system it must talk to, and the interface that system exposes
- Cleaning policy and the surfaces that policy excludes
- Pilot scope: how many units, in which department, for how long before the roll-out decision
Projects that arrive with this list usually move from enquiry to drawing in a week. Projects that arrive with only a photo of a machine take longer, because every one of these points has to be discovered by asking.

## Questions we are asked first
Can a hospital kiosk integrate with our existing HIS or booking system?
Do we need one kiosk model for registration and another for payment?
How is patient data handled on the terminal?
What is a realistic pilot before a full roll-out?

# Hotel Self Check-in Kiosks & Key Card Dispensing | Xinyuehong

URL: https://xinyuehongtech.com/industries/hotels/


# Hotel Self Check-in Kiosks & Key Card Dispensing
Check-in peaks between 15:00 and 19:00, when three arrivals want the same receptionist and one of them is a group of nine. A kiosk does not replace the desk; it takes the reservation that matches the booking exactly, so the desk can deal with the ones that do not.

## The 15:00 problem
A hotel check-in is four steps: identify the guest, confirm the reservation, take payment or incidentals, and hand over a key. Only the fourth step actually needs a physical thing to happen, and that is exactly where most self-service projects stall — the kiosk can read a passport, but it cannot encode a key card unless the dispenser is specified with the lock system.
Language is the second constraint. A city hotel may need four or five languages on the same screen, and the layout has to survive longer strings than the English version. If Arabic or Hebrew is on the list, the interface runs right-to-left and the screen height and font size are re-checked against that.
The third is the handover itself. A guest who checks in at 23:00 with a passport in one hand and a suitcase in the other needs the process to end in under two minutes, with a printed confirmation and a key card they can use immediately. If the kiosk produces a receipt but sends them to the desk for the key, the queue has not moved; it has just been split.

## Terminals for the lobby
Cabinets that carry passport reading, payment and printing in one footprint.
Passport MRZ reader option, national ID reader, camera bar and 80 mm printer for check-in and key issuing workflows.
Fits an existing reception desk where floor space is not available; card reader and printer optional.
Registration and check-in terminals compared by reader set and printing.

## What a hotel specification has to settle

### Passport MRZ and ID
MRZ reading is standard on a passport reader; chip reading depends on the module. Local ID cards need their own reader, and some markets require a scan of the document image rather than the data.

### Card dispensing and encoding
The key card system is the constraint. The kiosk needs a dispenser that takes your card stock and an encoder that talks to your lock vendor, and both are confirmed with that vendor before the cabinet is drawn The

### Room and incidentals
Card payment through a certified terminal, mounted on the cabinet. Pre-authorisation for incidentals is a PMS decision, not a kiosk one, but it changes the payment flow the customer sees.

### Reservation lookup
The kiosk needs a live connection to the PMS or the booking engine. Whether it can create a key for a reservation that has not been pre-authorised is a policy decision your revenue team has to make.

### Four languages, one layout
Longer strings break fixed-width buttons. The screen is chosen with the longest translated string in mind, and RTL languages change the whole layout rather than just the words.

### Lobby furniture
A floor-standing unit needs a power and network point, and a place that does not block the luggage flow. A countertop unit fits an existing desk but limits the peripheral stack.

## Procurement checklist
- Lock system and key card vendor, with the encoder model and its SDK
- Which documents are read: passport, national ID, residence permit, or all three
- Whether the kiosk may issue a key before the guest is pre-authorised
- Languages required, and the longest string in each
- PMS or booking engine interface, and who supports it after handover
- Lobby footprint, power and network position
- Branding: cabinet finish, logo placement and screen skin
- Pilot: one lobby, four to six weeks, measured on check-ins completed without staff

## Questions we are asked first
Can the kiosk issue a room key card?
Which identity documents can it read?
Does it work with our PMS?
Can the interface be in several languages?

# Parking Payment & Transport Kiosks | Xinyuehong

URL: https://xinyuehongtech.com/industries/parking-transport/


# Parking Payment & Transport Kiosks
A parking payment terminal is judged on a wet Tuesday: a driver stops, pays in under a minute and drives off. Every design decision — deck angle, screen brightness, ticket slot, plinth — follows from that one moment rather than from the screen.

## The payment deck is the whole design
Drivers arrive at an angle, often with the engine running. The card reader, contactless pad and ticket slot have to sit on one surface at one reach point; split them across the front face and the driver steps back, leans in, and leaves the card in the reader. That is why parking terminals are built around an angled deck rather than a vertical panel.
The screen has to survive a windscreen reflection and a low sun. Anti-glare glass and 500 to 1,000 nits are normal here, and the mounting orientation matters more than the panel specification: a screen facing east is unusable at 08:00 whatever its brightness.
The third issue is the weather. A kerbside unit sees rain at an angle, dust, salt in coastal cities and cleaning chemicals. The enclosure is sealed with a gasketed door, the cable entry is from below, and the plinth is bolted so the unit cannot be pushed out of alignment with the lane.

## Terminals for kerbside and station use
Payment decks and ticket printers in enclosures designed for outdoor queues.
Angled payment deck with card reader, contactless pad and ticket slot, in a weather-resistant enclosure on a plinth.
For station halls and interchanges where the unit stands indoors and needs a larger screen and full reader bay.
Ticket purchase and collection with QR scanning and contactless payment, for transport interchanges.

## What a parking specification has to settle

### Contactless and QR
Card and phone payment through a certified terminal, plus a QR scanner for app-based parking. Both sit on the deck, inside one reach envelope.

### Issue and collect
Some sites issue a ticket at entry and collect at exit; others are ticketless. The printer outlet and the scanner position follow from which model the operator runs.

### Rain, dust, salt
A sealed front, gasketed door and bottom cable entry. Coastal sites need stainless fixings; inland sites can use coated steel with a plinth.

### Sun and glare
Anti-glare glass, 500 to 1,000 nits, and an orientation chosen so the screen is not facing the rising or setting sun.

### Bolt-down plinth
A payment terminal is an obvious target for being struck or pushed. The plinth is bolted, and the service door is on the side away from the traffic lane.

### Parking system
The kiosk talks to the parking management system for tariffs and validation. Offline behaviour — what happens when the link drops — is a software decision that has to be agreed.

## Procurement checklist
- Kerbside, lane-side or in a station hall, and whether the position is covered
- Ticketless operation or ticket issue and collection
- Payment methods: contactless, chip, QR, cash
- Tariff and validation logic in the parking system, and offline behaviour
- Power and network at the plinth, and who provides the civil works
- Sun exposure and the direction the screen faces
- Cleaning regime and the chemicals used on the front face
- Service model: who clears a jam, who restocks paper, and the response time

## Questions we are asked first
Is the terminal suitable for an uncovered car park?
Can it work without tickets?
How is the unit fixed to the ground?
What happens when the network drops?
Can it take cash as well as cards?

# QSR Self-Ordering Kiosks for Fast Food & Fast Casual | Xinyuehong

URL: https://xinyuehongtech.com/industries/qsr-restaurants/


# QSR Self-Ordering Kiosks for Fast Food & Fast Casual
Lunch service is a throughput problem. At 12:30 the constraint is not the menu screen, it is how many orders a minute the counter can take. A kiosk earns its place only if it absorbs the simple orders, survives the grease and the heat, and prints a receipt without a staff member walking over.

## Where a quick-service queue actually breaks
Peak concurrency is the number that matters. Between 12:00 and 13:30 a single till may take three to four orders a minute, and a queue of twelve people forms in under five. A kiosk does not need to be faster than the till; it needs to take the orders that do not need a human — the standard combo, the repeat order, the item with one modifier.
The second break is accuracy, not speed. Order errors cost more than the extra minute they save, and every modifier is a chance to mishear. A touchscreen with a clear modifier path and a printed confirmation removes that failure mode entirely.
The third is environmental, and it is the one that kills cheap units. A restaurant back-of-house runs hot, and airborne grease settles on everything. A screen that needs wiping every hour, a printer that jams because the paper path is exposed, a PC with a fan pulling that air through the cabinet — these are the reasons an installed kiosk gets switched off in month four.

## Terminals for counter and floor
Two cabinet formats and one category overview, all quotable with your payment terminal and printer.
15.6-inch tilted terminal for counter ordering, with an optional card reader and 58 mm or 80 mm receipt printer.
32-inch 2560 x 1440 portrait screen with a glass scan deck, card readers and an 80 mm printer in the side column.
All ordering terminals in the range, compared by screen size, mounting and peripheral set.

## What the specification has to cover
Six items that decide whether the unit is still in service next summer.

### Size and angle
21.5 to 32 inches portrait, set at a 30-degree reading angle for a standing customer. A countertop unit suits a low counter; a floor-standing unit suits a queue that forms in front of the machine.

### Terminal bracket
Ingenico, Verifone and PAX devices mount on a plate cut to the specific model, with power and cable route inside the cabinet. The payment certification stays with the terminal.

### Printer duty cycle
80 mm thermal with an auto-cutter sized for the peak hour, not the daily average. Paper changes must be a front-door operation that a shift supervisor can do in under a minute.

### 2D code reader
A deck scanner reads coupon codes and loyalty QR codes at the same station as the order screen, so the customer does not handle paper twice.

### Grease and wipe-down
Flat glass, sealed edges and no fabric surfaces. The front face has to survive a degreaser wipe several times a day without the print wearing off.

### POS integration
Windows or Android, with the ordering application and its printer and payment SDKs confirmed before the cabinet is drawn. The kiosk is hardware; the POS logic stays in your stack.

## Procurement checklist
- Peak orders per hour, and how many of them are modifier-free
- The exact payment terminal model, so the bracket is cut once
- Receipt length and whether a second copy is printed for the kitchen
- Counter height and available footprint — countertop or floor-standing
- Cleaning chemicals used on the front face
- POS or ordering platform, and who owns the integration
- Languages on screen, and whether Arabic or another RTL language is required
- Pilot scope: two to four units in one site before a chain roll-out
Restaurant projects move fastest when the payment terminal is already chosen. The bracket, the cable route and the printer position all depend on it, and re-cutting a fascia is the most expensive change in the project.

Can the kiosk run our existing POS or ordering application?
Do you support Ingenico, Verifone and PAX payment terminals?
Countertop or floor-standing for a quick-service restaurant?
How do you handle heat and grease in the kitchen area?

# Retail Self-Checkout & Self-Service Kiosks | Xinyuehong

URL: https://xinyuehongtech.com/industries/retail/


# Retail Self-Checkout & Self-Service Kiosks
A self-checkout lane is judged on two numbers: items scanned per minute and interventions per hundred transactions. Every hardware decision — scan window, screen height, bagging space, payment position — moves one of those numbers.

## Scan, pay, bag, repeat
Self-checkout fails on exceptions, not on normal baskets. A barcode that will not read, a loose item with no label, an age-restricted product — each one needs a staff member, and if the station is badly laid out the staff member has to walk around the unit to help. The cabinet layout should let one person assist two lanes without pushing past a queue.
The scan deck is the part that gets overlooked. A window that is flush with the counter, lit, and angled toward the customer cuts the number of failed scans more than a faster processor does. A 2D imager that reads phone screens matters as much as one that reads printed labels, because loyalty and payment codes now arrive on a phone.
Payment position is the other decision. Putting the terminal on the same side as the scanner keeps the customer's hands in one place; putting it on the far side forces a reach across the bagging area, which is where cards get left behind. In unattended lanes, the payment terminal is also the part most exposed to tampering, so the mounting has to be serviceable by staff but not removable by a customer.

## Terminals for the shop floor
Countertop, floor-standing and wall-mounted cabinets, with the scanner and payment deck positioned for one-handed use.
Payment-ready cabinets with scanner, printer and third-party payment device mounting.
Illuminated scan window, card and ID reader bay and an 80 mm printer, for high-traffic lanes.
Compact terminals for narrow aisles and service counters where a floor-standing lane will not fit.

## What the specification has to settle

### Scan window
Flush, lit and angled toward the customer. 1D and 2D reading in the same module, so printed labels and phone screens both work without a second device.

### Terminal position
Same side as the scanner, reachable without crossing the bagging area. The mounting plate is cut for the acquirer's device, and the cable route is inside the cabinet so it cannot be unplugged by a customer.

### Receipt or digital
80 mm thermal with auto-cutter where a paper receipt is still expected; a QR on screen where the chain has moved to digital receipts. Both can coexist, with the printer as an option.

### Height and reach
Screen and scan deck set for a standing adult, with the payment terminal inside the same reach envelope. Trolley users and wheelchair users change the height range, and that is a drawing decision.

### Camera and tamper
A front camera above the display supports loss prevention and age checks. In unattended lanes the payment device and the cash aperture are the parts that need the strongest mounting.

### POS and loyalty
The kiosk is hardware: the POS application drives scanning, payment and printing. Loyalty lookup runs through the same application, and the scanner has to read the phone screen the loyalty code arrives on.

## Procurement checklist
- Items per basket and expected items per minute at peak
- The exact payment device, and whether it must be customer-removable for servicing
- Whether a paper receipt is still issued, or the chain has moved to digital
- Bagging area dimensions and the trolley or basket flow
- Age-restricted products, and how the station calls for authorisation
- Loss-prevention camera requirements and where footage is stored
- POS platform and loyalty integration owner
- Pilot: one store, two lanes, four weeks, measured on interventions per hundred baskets

## Questions we are asked first
Is this a complete self-checkout lane or only the kiosk?
Can the scanner read phone screens for loyalty and payment codes?
Which payment terminals can be mounted?
Can the kiosk be used unattended, for example in a 24-hour store?

## Where this build fits in a branch
A branch floor is planned around a queue rather than a machine, and this unit is sized for that: the 27-inch portrait screen sits at standing eye level, while the PIN pad and card readers are set on a shelf below the sight line so the next customer cannot read a balance over the user's shoulder. The privacy hood belongs to the encrypting PIN pad module itself rather than to the cabinet skin.
When statement printing, PIN changes and balance enquiries move off the counter, the counter is left free for account opening and advice. The three-tile layout follows that order of work: service selection at the top, payment hardware in the middle, receipt at the bottom, so a customer who has never used the terminal can finish without staff direction.
The base runs on braked castors, which means a branch can re-plan its lobby without a rigging team, and the lockable service door keeps paper and module access separate from the cash-free service area. For a pilot branch the same cabinet can be quoted with one reader set, then extended to a fuller module mix once the flow is proven.

# Border Inspection Service Island

Further modules — cash handling, A4 document printing, NFC, barcode scanning, card dispensing, custom keypads or a second display — can also be reviewed on request.

## Typical applications

### Port and land-crossing lanes with mixed credential types

### Immigration halls issuing permits and collecting fees

### Multi-step traveller processing before the counter

## How the island works in a checkpoint hall
Checkpoint halls rarely handle one credential type. A single queue can contain ID cards, bank cards, permits and travel documents, and the four reader slots on this island are there to absorb that mix instead of sending people to different machines. Which reader goes in which slot is decided per project, so the module set follows the credential mix of the hall rather than the other way round.
The 21.5-inch guidance display above the 32-inch working screen is not decoration. It carries the next-step instruction, the lane status and the notice that would otherwise need a member of staff standing beside the unit, which is what makes a multi-step process work without supervision.
The cabinet is an island rather than a pedestal: consumables, cabling and the service panels sit inside the body, and the base can be bolted down where the hall layout is fixed. The full-size keyboard and contactless pad on the counter deck are positioned for the standing posture a traveller takes when they arrive with a bag in one hand.

## Typical applications

### Community clinic registration and card issue

## Card issue at a community clinic
This build exists for one task that most kiosks cannot do: hand a physical card to the patient. The motorised hopper holds around 100 cards and reports empty and jam states, so clinic staff know when to reload without opening the cabinet to look. That matters in a community clinic where the terminal is checked once in the morning and once at closing.
Registration and card issue are usually the first two steps of a visit, and both are on this unit: contactless and ID reading identify the patient, the dispenser issues the card, and the 80 mm printer produces the slip that carries the queue number. A patient who arrives without an appointment can complete the whole sequence at the machine.
The cabinet is cold-rolled steel with a lockable service door, sized to sit in a waiting area rather than a back office. Replenishment is a front-door operation: the hopper pulls out, a new stack drops in, and the sensor confirms the count before the unit returns to service.

## A desk-side terminal, not a lobby machine
This is the smallest unit in the range and it is deliberately not a floor-standing kiosk. A 15.6-inch screen set at a 30-degree operating angle on a counter puts the interface at the height of a seated or leaning user, which is the posture people take at a reception desk, a retail counter or a clinic check-in point.
Because it sits on furniture the venue already owns, it avoids the floor space, power trench and barrier planning that a full kiosk needs. The cable exit is at the rear, so the unit can be pushed back against a wall or a screen without a visible loom, and the optional clamp or bolt-down plate keeps it in place where the counter is shared with other equipment.
The honest limit is throughput. One person at a time, standing at a counter, is the design case; for a queue that forms in front of the unit, a floor-standing model with a larger screen and a lower peripheral deck is the better answer. Used within that limit, this is the cheapest way to put a working interface in front of customers.

### Citizen service halls and one-stop centres

## Two screens, two audiences
A citizen service hall has two audiences at the same machine: the person operating it and the person waiting behind them. The 23.8-inch working screen faces the user, while the 21.5-inch screen above it faces the room and carries guidance, notices and service information. That split keeps the working flow uncluttered without leaving the queue uninformed.
The reader bank is built for documents rather than cards alone: national ID, social-security card and bank card readers sit in one module bank, with a front camera module above the main screen for face capture where the service requires it. Certificate printing and payment both come out of the same 80 mm printer, so a citizen can finish a transaction in one visit.
Halls that deploy this unit usually do so in banks of three or four, which changes the requirement: the cabinet footprint, the service door swing and the height of the reader bank all need to work when units stand side by side. The floor-standing base with lockable castors allows a bank to be re-arranged when the hall is reconfigured.

## Permit work before the counter
Exit-entry halls deal with a small number of processes repeated at volume: permit application, fee payment, and collection of the permit, endorsement or receipt. This build is arranged around that sequence, with a 32-inch working screen and a large cabinet that keeps consumables and an optional A4 printer out of the public side of the unit.
The 21.5-inch upper display carries queue status and public notices, which is what allows the unit to stand in a hall rather than beside a staffed desk. The reader set covers IC, ID and bank cards, with a document reader added where the application needs passport or travel-document data.
The cabinet is deliberately large. A4 form printing, a full module stack and the cable management for a hall installation all need volume, and a slim body would force a separate printer table next to the kiosk. The trade-off is floor area, which is why the base runs on lockable castors for cleaning and re-layout.

## Typical applications

## Security first, then service
The design of this unit starts from the assumption that it will hold value. The 19-inch screen is recessed into a deep fascia with an anti-peep surround, the encrypting PIN pad sits on its own secure module, and the cabinet uses a vault-style service door with mounting points for an alarm or a security seal. Those choices cost screen area and cabinet depth, and they are the reason the unit looks the way it does.
Functionally it is a cashless or cash-handling terminal depending on the module fitted: EMV chip and magnetic-stripe reading as standard, contactless as an option, and a cash acceptor or document aperture behind the secure fascia where the branch needs deposit or withdrawal. Card issuance and PIN change are the other common uses.
It suits a self-service corner inside an existing branch rather than a standalone lobby, because the plinth can be bolted down and the service access is designed for a two-person cash-handling procedure. Where the site has no secure back room, a cash-handling build should not be specified at all.

## Typical applications

### Transport halls and attraction entrances

### Hospital service lobbies with queue tickets

### Government service centre ticket counters

## Issuing the ticket, not just the number
Queue-ticket terminals fail in one of two ways: the printer jams at the busiest hour, or the outlet is placed where the ticket falls on the floor. This build addresses both mechanically. The 32-inch vertical screen stands at head height, and the 80 mm printer has a dedicated outlet with an auto-cutter, so the ticket is presented rather than ejected.
The QR and barcode scanner at the deck lets the same unit serve collection as well as issue: a visitor who booked online scans the confirmation and receives a printed queue number, which means one machine covers walk-in and pre-booked traffic without a second terminal.
It is used in transport halls, attraction entrances and hospital lobbies, and the common requirement is not the screen but the paper path. Ticket stock, cutter life and the height of the outlet are the parts that decide whether the installation survives a busy Saturday, so they are specified with the venue's throughput in mind rather than as defaults.

## Document-led service in a municipal hall
Most government service transactions begin with a document rather than a card. This build puts an ID document reader with MRZ and second-generation ID support at the centre of the unit, then surrounds it with the card readers a municipal hall actually uses: social-security card, bank card and a contactless pad for the payment step.
The 27-inch portrait screen is tall enough to show a form or a certificate preview above the reader deck without the user having to step back, which matters in a hall where the next person in the queue is standing close behind. The 80 mm printer issues receipts and short certificates; longer documents are usually printed at a staffed counter.
Because the same cabinet is deployed by different agencies, the reader set is the variable. A social-security counter may need only the card slot, while a records desk needs the document reader and a scanner. The cabinet and the harness accept both without a re-draw, which keeps spares and training consistent across a hall.

## Outpatient hall, first contact
In an outpatient hall the kiosk is usually the patient's first contact with the hospital that day, and the queue behind them is the constraint. This build pairs a 32-inch working screen with a 21.5-inch guidance screen above it, so appointment check-in, registration and payment can run while the guidance screen shows the queue number and the direction to the consulting room.
The retractable keyboard with stainless-steel keycaps is there for the cases a touchscreen handles badly: an ID number, a phone number, a date of birth entered by an older patient. It retracts flush when not in use, which keeps the front face clean enough to wipe down between users.
Payment hardware covers IC, ID and bank cards with a contactless option, and the 80 mm printer issues the slip that carries the queue number. Consumables are reached from the front, so a ward clerk can change paper without moving the cabinet or calling an engineer.

## Enquiry, validation and printout
Medical insurance counters deal with a narrow set of tasks at high volume: check the balance, confirm the claim status, validate the card, print the statement. This build is arranged around that loop, with social-security, ID and bank card readers at the deck and a document scanner under the display for the paper forms that still arrive at the counter.
The curved portrait screen is a practical choice rather than a styling one. At 27 inches it fills the standing field of view without the top edge falling outside it, so a user reading a long list of claim items does not have to step back, and the reflection from ceiling lights is spread across the curve instead of concentrating in one band.
The cabinet is a standard floor-standing body on lockable castors, which means the same model can be used in a hall, a corridor outside an insurance office or a community service point. Only the reader set and the software change between those sites.

## A printing station, with an identity check
This unit is essentially a secure printer with a screen attached, and it is specified that way. A 21.5-inch touchscreen sits above an A4 laser or thermal document printer with a collection slot, and the cabinet is sized around the paper path so a full report can be printed and collected without the user reaching into the machine.
Because medical records are involved, the identity step comes before the print. IC and ID card readers verify the patient, and the front camera captures a record photo where the hospital's policy requires one. The screen then shows what is about to be printed, so the patient confirms the document set before any paper is released.
The cabinet has front paper access. That sounds like a detail until the alternative is understood: a rear-loading printer forces the unit away from the wall and into the corridor, which is exactly where a hospital cannot afford to lose space.

## Typical applications

### Inpatient floors for bedside payment

### Temporary screening and triage points

### Discharge settlement desks

## When the machine has to come to the patient
Most hospital kiosks assume the patient can walk to the lobby. This one assumes they cannot. The 27-inch screen and the payment hardware are mounted on a station with four braked castors, a cable management reel and a transport lock, so it can be moved to a ward, a temporary screening point or a discharge desk and then locked in place for the session.
The second 21.5-inch screen sits on the camera column and faces away from the operator, which lets a nurse or clerk run the session while the patient sees the same information. That arrangement is what makes bedside payment workable: the patient is not asked to lean over a terminal from a bed.
The engineering effort in a mobile unit is not the screen, it is the cable. A reel that pays out and retracts without trapping, a transport lock that survives a lift, and a cabinet that stays stable when a patient leans on it are the parts that decide whether the station is used or left in a corridor.

## One cabinet, several industries
This is the largest terminal in the range and the one specified when a project cannot yet say which industry it will end up in. The 32-inch 2560 × 1440 portrait screen carries a full application rather than a tile menu, the scanner is set into an illuminated window below the display, and the card reader bay handles IC, ID and bank cards with a national ID reader where the module supports it.
The QHD resolution matters at this size. At arm's length a 32-inch 1080p panel shows visible pixels on small form text, which is exactly what a passport number, a bank account field or a hotel key-code screen contains. The higher pixel density keeps those fields legible without enlarging the interface.
The body is brushed stainless steel with a tempered glass counter deck, chosen because the unit stands in public halls where the front surface is touched, leaned on and cleaned hundreds of times a day. Powder-coated steel marks and dulls at that level of use; stainless steel does not. Modules are accessible from a separate lockable service door, so maintenance does not expose the payment bay.

## Typical applications

### Shopping mall and airport car parks

## Kerbside hardware, not lobby hardware
A payment terminal in a car park is judged by what happens on a wet Tuesday, not by its screen. This build puts the hardware behind a steel enclosure with a weather-resistant front option, mounts it on a floor plinth for kerbside or lane-side installation, and angles the payment deck so a driver standing at the machine can present a card, a phone or a ticket without bending down.
The 21.5-inch portrait display carries the amount due and the exit instruction, with anti-glare glass because most parking machines face a road or a windscreen. The scanner reads 1D barcodes and 2D QR codes for printed tickets and app-based parking codes, so the same unit serves both paper and phone users.
The design constraint that shapes everything else is the deck: card reader, contactless pad and ticket slot are grouped on one angled surface at a single reach point. Splitting them across the front face would force the driver to step back and lean in, which is how cards get left in readers.

## Built for corridors
Social-security service points are often corridors and waiting areas rather than purpose-built halls, and a standard kiosk depth does not fit those spaces. This cabinet reduces depth to the point where the unit can stand against a corridor wall without narrowing the walking route, while keeping a 21.5-inch portrait screen at reading height.
The module set is deliberately complete for a narrow body: social-security card slot, ID scanner, bank card reader, QR scanner and a compact stainless keyboard for the numbers that a touchscreen handles badly. The 80 mm printer issues balance statements and certificates from the same front face.
Slimming a kiosk usually means moving the printer or the PC into a separate box beside it. Here the components are re-stacked vertically inside the column, which is why the service door opens on the narrow side and why paper access is a front operation. It is a tighter assembly to build, and it is the reason this model exists as a separate cabinet rather than an option.

## Wayfinding at a standing reader's angle
A horizontal screen is the right shape for a map, a floor plan or a directory, and the wrong shape for a standing user unless it is tilted. This unit sets a 32-inch horizontal touchscreen into a curved enclosure at a sloped reading angle, so a visitor can look down at a plan the way they would look at a printed map on a lectern.
The weighted floor base is part of that design. A sloped screen invites people to lean on the front edge, and a light base would move under that load. The curve also hides the transition between the screen bezel and the enclosure, which matters in a lobby where the unit is part of the furniture rather than a utility.
For museums and exhibition spaces the same cabinet can carry a wheelchair-height second screen, and for retail directories the module bay accepts an NFC pad or a receipt printer. The unit is normally specified without payment hardware, because its job is to answer a question rather than to complete a transaction.

## Two outlets, one queue
Buying a ticket and collecting one are different transactions with different failure modes, and this cabinet separates them physically. The thermal printer issues new tickets through one outlet, while a separate collection outlet presents pre-paid tickets after the QR scanner reads the booking. Two outlets mean a collection does not queue behind a purchase.
The 32-inch vertical screen carries the journey or event selection, and the contactless reader handles card and phone payment with a bank card reader option where the venue's acquirer requires a chip read. The cabinet is cold-rolled steel with a lockable service door, sized for a station hall where the unit stands beside a barrier line.
Station and venue halls usually deploy these in banks of two or three, positioned so the collection outlet faces the flow of arriving passengers and the purchase screen faces the concourse. That orientation is worth deciding before the cabinets are ordered, because it changes which side the service door opens on.

## Payment where the corridor already is
Not every payment point can afford floor space. This terminal fixes to a wall bracket or VESA plate with rear cable entry, so a ward corridor, a lift lobby or the space beside a nurse station gains a payment point without losing a metre of circulation.
The 21.5-inch touchscreen is set at the height the hospital chooses, which is the advantage a wall mount has over a floor-standing unit: the same model can serve a standing adult in a lift lobby and a seated patient beside a ward, simply by fixing it at a different height. The encrypting PIN pad with its privacy hood is on the unit rather than on a separate pedestal, and the 80 mm printer presents the receipt at the bottom edge.
The constraint to plan for is services. A wall position needs power and network inside the wall or in a surface trunking run, and retrofitting that into a finished corridor is the expensive part of the project. Where the services already exist, this is the least disruptive way to add self-payment to a floor.

# Floor-Standing vs Wall-Mounted Kiosks | Xinyuehong

URL: https://xinyuehongtech.com/news/floor-standing-vs-wall-mounted-kiosks/

# Floor-Standing vs Wall-Mounted Kiosks
By
## Start with the footprint, not the cabinet
A floor-standing terminal needs a footprint of roughly 350 by 450 mm for a single-screen unit and 500 by 600 mm once a printer, a document reader and a cash module share the base. The number that actually decides the position is the clear space in front: a wheelchair user needs a 30 by 48 inch approach, and a standing queue needs about 1.2 m from the screen to the next person's toes. Measure that before the cabinet is drawn; it eliminates more positions than the cabinet dimensions ever will.
A wall-mounted unit is a different calculation. The cabinet is typically 100 to 250 mm deep, so the corridor keeps its width, but the wall has to carry 40 to 90 kg at an eccentric load. That means blocking or a steel sub-frame behind the finish, not plasterboard anchors. If the wall is a glazed partition or a drywall demountable system, budget for a frame and a structural check.
## Viewing height decides the screen size
ADA 308 and 309 ask for controls within 15 to 48 inches above the finished floor; a comfortable screen centre for a standing adult lands around 1,200 to 1,400 mm. A floor-standing cabinet reaches that height with a stand, which is why a 27-inch portrait screen reads comfortably while a 21.5-inch landscape does not. A wall-mounted unit usually sits at 1,100 to 1,200 mm centre and needs a shallower viewing cone — fine for a 21.5-inch screen at 500 to 700 mm viewing distance, tight for anything larger.
Two practical consequences follow. On a floor-standing unit, spend the height budget on the screen and put the printer outlet below 1,200 mm so the ticket is reachable without bending. On a wall-mounted unit, keep the reading and printing tasks separate: put the printer in a pedestal or a counter below the screen rather than hanging it at shoulder height.
## Where the hardware goes
Inside a floor-standing cabinet there is room for the computing platform, a receipt printer, a document or card module, a UPS and the cable slack that service work needs. That space is the real reason floor-standing units dominate multi-function kiosks: a 32-inch terminal with five modules needs a cabinet volume a wall unit cannot offer.
A wall-mounted unit is limited to shallow modules — a card reader, a QR scanner, a contactless pad, a small thermal printer. When the computing platform will not fit, it goes into a ceiling void, a riser cupboard or a nearby comms cabinet, and the run to the screen becomes a design constraint: keep USB and video runs under the limits your platform supports, and specify shielded cable if the run passes near mains wiring.
## Service access and consumables
Every kiosk needs someone to change paper, clear a jam, wipe the screen and reboot it. On a floor-standing unit, a front-hinged door with a lock is the default; a rear door only works if the unit stands away from the wall, which conflicts with queue geometry more often than expected. On a wall-mounted unit, the service door usually swings forward, so the same 900 mm of clear floor that serves the wheelchair user serves the technician.
Count the consumable events before choosing the style. A busy ticket counter may reload a printer three times a day; a check-in terminal once a week. High-consumable tasks favour a floor-standing cabinet with a large roll and a front door. Low-consumable tasks — a directory, a card enquiry — tolerate a wall unit.
## Traffic pattern and queue geometry
Floor-standing terminals form queues well because people can approach from three sides and the screen faces the aisle. Wall-mounted terminals serve better as side tasks: a payment at the end of a counter, a check-in in a corridor, a wayfinding point beside a lift lobby. The failure mode for a wall unit is a queue that forms along the wall and blocks the corridor behind it.
Watch the approach angle too. A screen set flat against a wall is read at 90 degrees, which is fine for a short interaction and tiring for a two-minute form. A floor-standing cabinet can be rotated five to ten degrees toward the approach path, which costs nothing at drawing stage and removes a whole class of complaints.
## Installation cost and structure
Floor-standing units cost more to ship and less to install: a plinth or levelling feet, a power point and a network drop. Wall-mounted units cost less to ship and more to install: a structural survey, blocking, a licensed installer, and a lift if the wall is above ground floor. On a multi-site roll-out the difference compounds — a wall unit that needs a survey per site can add weeks to a schedule.
The decision table below summarises the trade-off. Use it as a first filter, then confirm against the actual site drawing.
Choosing between the two installation styles
Factor
Floor-standing
Wall-mounted

# Hotel Check-in Kiosk Hardware: Peripherals and Enclosure

URL: https://xinyuehongtech.com/news/hotel-kiosk-peripherals-enclosure/


# Hotel Check-in Kiosk Hardware: Peripherals and Enclosure
By
A hotel check-in kiosk looks like a software project and is actually a peripheral-integration project. The screen is settled in a week; the key card encoder, the passport reader and the lock vendor decide whether the unit works at all. Then the enclosure has to fit all of it, survive a lobby, and look like it belongs to the brand.

## The short version
Four peripherals decide the build: a passport or ID reader, a key card dispenser with an encoder that matches the lock system, a camera for identity capture, and a receipt printer. The payment terminal is mounted, not integrated. The enclosure is 1.2 to 2.0 mm cold-rolled steel, laser cut and CNC bent, powder coated at 60 to 80 microns, and it takes three to six weeks from approved CAD to a finished batch — one to two weeks for the drawing, two to three for a prototype.

## Part 1: the peripheral stack
What each peripheral needs, and where hotel projects usually stall.
Peripheral
What it needs from the project
Where it stalls
Passport / ID reader
MRZ reading as standard; chip reading depends on the module; local ID cards need their own reader
Assuming MRZ covers every document, when the property also accepts national IDs or residence permits
Key card dispenser and encoder
A dispenser sized for your card stock, and an encoder that talks to the lock system
The lock vendor is engaged after the cabinet is drawn, and the encoder does not fit the bay
Camera
Position above the display at face height, with the field of view set for a standing guest
Camera added as an afterthought, giving a chin-level view and unusable captures
Receipt printer
80 mm thermal with auto-cutter, paper accessible from the front
Paper change needs a technician, so staff stop using the printer
Payment terminal
Mounted on a plate cut for the exact device, with power and data inside the cabinet
Treated as part of the kiosk, so the certification and the bracket are both wrong

### The key card problem is a vendor problem
Most hotel self-service projects fail here, and not because the hardware is bad. A key card is issued by an encoder that must be certified or licensed by the lock system vendor — ASSA ABLOY, Salto, Onity and Dormakaba all have their own encoder families and their own integration paths. The kiosk factory can provide the bay, the power and the serial link, but it cannot make a third-party encoder talk to a lock system without that vendor in the room.
The practical sequence is: lock vendor first, encoder model second, kiosk bay third. Projects that start with the cabinet usually end up with a dispenser that issues blank cards, which is worse than no kiosk at all.

### Identity capture is a policy question as much as a hardware one
Reading a passport MRZ gives you name, number and dates. Reading the chip gives you a signed record. Scanning the photo page gives you an image that a human may have to review. Which of those the property is allowed to store, and for how long, is set by local data-protection rules and by the hotel group's own policy — and it changes the reader specification. A property that only needs to verify a name does not need a chip reader.

## Part 2: from CAD to powder coating
An enclosure is a sequence of processes, and each one has a tolerance that accumulates. The chain for a kiosk cabinet is: laser cutting, CNC bending, welding or riveting, surface pretreatment, powder coating, then assembly and test.

### Cutting and bending
Sheet is normally 1.2 to 2.0 mm cold-rolled steel for a painted cabinet, or 1.5 mm stainless where the front face is touched constantly and must not chip. Laser cutting holds roughly ±0.1 mm on a profile; CNC bending holds roughly ±0.2 mm on a bend position, and the tolerance grows with the number of bends in a chain. That is why a drawing that stacks six bends to position a card slot is a drawing that will need a slotted hole, not a round one.

### Finishing
Powder coating is where appearance and durability are decided. The pretreatment matters more than the powder: degreasing, phosphating and a rinse before coating is what stops a cabinet from rusting at a scratch two years later. Coating thickness is typically 60 to 80 microns, and colour is matched against a physical sample rather than a screen, because the same RAL number looks different in a lobby at 3000 K and in a factory under daylight.

### Prototype, then batch
Typical schedule for a custom enclosure, counted from the approved brief.
Stage
Duration
What is fixed at the end of it
CAD and drawing approval
1 – 2 weeks
Peripheral positions, service access, cable routes, material and finish
Prototype build
2 – 3 weeks
Fit of every module, coating sample, label positions
Validation
1 – 2 weeks
Burn-in, thermal check, customer sign-off on the sample
Production batch
3 – 4 weeks
Fixtures and bending programs reused, batch coating, final inspection
The economics change between prototype and batch. A single unit carries the full programming and setup cost; a batch of fifty amortises the same work across the run. What does not amortise is new tooling — a weld fixture or a custom extrusion is a one-off that stays a one-off, and it is quoted separately for that reason.

## What drives cost in the enclosure

- The full peripheral list, with model numbers where already chosen
- Lock system and encoder, confirmed with that vendor in writing
- Documents the reader must accept, and what may be stored
- Cabinet material, colour reference and finish (painted, stainless, brushed)
- Mounting: floor-standing with plinth, wall bracket, or countertop
- Ingress and impact requirements, which decide gaskets and glass (
- Branding: logo file, placement, and whether it is printed, etched or a badge
- Prototype quantity, batch quantity, and the date the first unit has to be on site
