# How to Choose a Self-Service Kiosk | Xinyuehong

URL: https://xinyuehongtech.com/news/how-to-choose-a-self-service-kiosk/

# How to Choose a Self-Service Kiosk
By
## Start from the transaction, not the catalogue
Write the transaction down as a sequence of steps and time each one. A wayfinding lookup is 15 seconds and never touches a printer. A restaurant order is 90 seconds, ends with two receipts and often a payment card. A hospital registration is two to three minutes, needs an ID document, a payment and a printed slip. Those three numbers — 15 seconds, 90 seconds, three minutes — set the screen size, the peripheral list and the cabinet size far more reliably than a product photo.
Note the error paths at the same time. What happens when the card is declined, the passport chip cannot be read, or the printer is empty? A kiosk that handles the happy path in 30 seconds and the failure path in five minutes will generate staff interventions, and staff interventions are the cost that kills the business case.
## Match the screen to the task
Screen size follows the amount of information the customer has to read and the number of targets they have to hit. A directory or a single-question check-in works on 15.6 to 21.5 inches in landscape. A food menu with modifiers needs 21.5 to 27 inches, portrait, because the category rail and the basket both want horizontal space. A multi-service terminal — immigration, banking, hotel, retail in one cabinet — goes to 32 inches with a QHD panel so two content zones can coexist without shrinking the type.
Mounting height matters as much as size. Controls between 15 and 48 inches above the finished floor satisfy ADA 308, and a screen centre around 1,200 to 1,400 mm suits a standing adult. Portrait orientation puts more of the screen inside that band. If the unit also serves seated users, plan a 30 by 48 inch clear floor in front of it and keep the primary buttons in the lower half.
## List the peripherals with their interfaces
Write the list as a table with four columns: module, model, interface, who supplies the driver. Most integration surprises come from that last column. A receipt printer may be USB with a vendor SDK, a serial device with a virtual COM port, or a network printer that needs a fixed IP. A passport reader may present itself as a keyboard wedge or require a full SDK. A payment terminal is its own certified device and connects over USB, serial or Ethernet depending on the provider.
Separate mandatory modules from optional ones before you ask for prices. A quote that lists every possible module is not comparable to one that lists the required set. Payment is the clearest example: the terminal, its certification and its integration are usually supplied through an acquirer, so the kiosk's job is to provide a mounting position, power and a data path — not to certify the payment application.
## Decide the operating system from the software, not the hardware
Windows suits applications that depend on a full driver stack — serial devices, legacy POS clients, USB peripherals with Windows-only SDKs. Android suits content-led applications, digital signage and web apps, and boots faster, but the vendor's Android build and its peripheral support have to be confirmed module by module. Linux suits teams with in-house engineering and a fixed peripheral set.
The practical test is a list: for every module, does the chosen platform have a driver and a supported SDK? If two modules only exist on Windows, the decision is made for you. If the application is a browser page and the peripherals are USB HID, Android will usually cost less to run.
## Check the deployment conditions
Indoor lobby and outdoor kerbside are different machines. Indoor units can use a standard front face; wet or dusty positions need a sealed front and a defined IP rating, and public unsupervised sites need an impact rating for the glass. Brightness is the other variable: 400 to 500 nits is fine under a ceiling, 700 to 1,000 nits is normal for a screen that faces daylight, and anti-glare glass matters more than the peak figure.
Also confirm the duty cycle. A terminal that runs 24/7 with no restart window needs industrial components and a thermal design that removes heat without a fan; a terminal that runs eight hours a day in a staffed lobby can be built closer to commercial hardware.
## Compare quotations on the same basis
Ask for a quotation in the module structure you defined, with each line marked included, optional or excluded. Freight, duties, installation, software integration and the spare-parts kit are the five lines most often left out, and they are the five that change the total. A quote that states the certification scope per module is worth more than one that says "CE certified" without saying for what.
## Pilot before volume
Run two to four units for four to six weeks and measure transactions per unit per day, average session time, intervention rate and the top three failure reasons. Those four numbers decide the roll-out mix better than any specification review. They also tell you whether the screen was the right size — if staff are regularly leaning in to press a button, it was not.

# Kiosk ADA Height, IP65 and IK Ratings Explained | Xinyuehong

URL: https://xinyuehongtech.com/news/kiosk-ada-ip-ik-ratings/


# Kiosk ADA Height, IP65 and IK Ratings Explained
By
Three numbers decide most of the mechanical design of a public terminal: the reach range the users have to work within, the ingress protection the site demands, and the impact energy the front glass has to survive. Get them wrong and the cabinet is rebuilt; get them right at drawing stage and they cost almost nothing.

## The three constraints at a glance
Reference values. Local codes and the client's own accessibility policy always take precedence.
Constraint
Standard
Number that matters
Reach range
ADA 2010, sections 308 and 309 (US); EN 301 549 and ISO 21542 elsewhere
Operable parts between
Clear floor space
ADA 305
Ingress protection
IEC 60529
Impact resistance
IEC 62262

## ADA: what the standard actually asks of a kiosk
The Americans with Disabilities Act is a US civil-rights law, and its 2010 Standards for Accessible Design set dimensional rules that apply to self-service equipment in places of public accommodation. The two sections that matter most for a kiosk are 308, which defines reach ranges, and 309, which defines how an operable part must work.
In practice this produces four requirements on the drawing:
Two practical consequences. First, if the same terminal serves standing adults and wheelchair users, either the whole interactive zone is lowered and the screen tilted, or a second lower screen is added — the

## IP ratings: the two digits, decoded
IP codes come from IEC 60529. The first digit is solids, the second is water, and a higher number always includes the lower ones. Only the first digit goes to 6; the second can go to 9K.
Ingress protection levels that appear in kiosk specifications.
Rating
Solids
Water
Where it is appropriate
IP54
Dust protected
Splashing water
Covered corridors, hospital wards, office lobbies
IP65
Dust tight
Water jets from a nozzle
Wash-down areas, covered outdoor bays, food production
IP66
Dust tight
Powerful water jets
Exposed kerbside units, vehicle wash-down zones
The rating applies to the enclosure as tested, not to the whole machine in service. A unit rated IP65 with the service door open is not IP65, and a cable gland left loose at installation cancels the rating just as effectively. That is why the specification should say which surfaces carry the rating — front face only, or the complete cabinet — and how the cable entry is sealed.
For an indoor terminal in a dry hall, IP54 is enough and cheaper. For anything that will be hosed down or rained on, the front face needs a sealed bezel and the rear needs a gasketed door; the

## IK ratings: impact, not water
IK codes come from IEC 62262 and describe how much mechanical impact the enclosure survives, expressed in joules. IK08 is 5 joules, roughly a 1.7 kg mass dropped from 30 cm; IK10 is 20 joules, roughly a 5 kg mass from 40 cm.
On a kiosk the rating is really a statement about two different things: the cover glass, and the cabinet shell. A 3 mm chemically strengthened glass can pass IK08 while a 6 mm annealed glass of the same size may not, because the failure is about how the glass breaks, not how thick it is. The shell matters for the corners and the service door, which is where a trolley or a delivery cart usually lands.
For unsupervised sites — a station forecourt, a 24-hour lobby, a car park — IK10 on the front glass and a bolted plinth are the normal combination. In a staffed hospital corridor, IK08 is usually sufficient and the money is better spent on the touch stack.

## Brightness and touch in daylight
Brightness is measured in nits (cd/m²). A standard indoor panel runs 250 to 350 nits; a window-facing lobby needs 500 to 700; direct sunlight needs 1,000 or more, plus an anti-reflective treatment, or the screen becomes a mirror.
Typical brightness targets by position.
Position
Brightness
Note
Indoor hall, no daylight
250 – 350 nits
Standard panel, lowest cost
Lobby or corridor with windows
500 – 700 nits
Anti-glare glass, auto brightness
Covered outdoor bay
1,000 nits
Light sensor, thermal management
Direct sun
1,500 – 2,500 nits
Heated or cooled enclosure, IR touch often preferred
Touch technology interacts with the environment. Projected capacitive (PCAP) gives the best image and multi-touch, but a thick glove or a film of water breaks contact. Infrared touch works through gloves and scratches less visibly, at the cost of a deeper bezel and sensitivity to dust on the frame. Resistive still has a place where the operator wears heavy gloves and uses a stylus.
Heat is the other half of the outdoor problem. A sealed enclosure in direct sun can sit 20 to 30 °C above ambient inside, which is why outdoor units are usually specified with an air-conditioned or heat-exchanger cabinet rather than a fan, and why the panel's operating temperature range is quoted separately from the enclosure's.

## How these constraints reach the sheet metal
None of the above is a software problem, and all of it lands on the drawing:
- The interactive zone is set by the reach range, which sets the cabinet height and the screen tilt — not the other way round.
- IP rating sets the door gasket, the cable gland, the seam welding and the powder-coat coverage on cut edges.
- IK rating sets the glass specification, the bezel retention and the plinth fixings.
- Brightness and heat set the panel, the glass coating and whether the cabinet carries a heat exchanger.
- All of it changes the maintenance access, which is why the service door is usually the last thing drawn and the first thing to regret.
If the project is a standard cabinet, these are options and the quotation lists them. If the project is a new enclosure, they are inputs to the CAD model, and changing them after the first prototype is what turns a four-week build into a twelve-week one.

How bright does an outdoor kiosk screen need to be?

# EMV Terminal Integration and Kiosk OS Choice | Xinyuehong

URL: https://xinyuehongtech.com/news/kiosk-payment-integration-os/


# Integrating a Payment Terminal into a Kiosk
By
Payment is the part of a kiosk project that most often arrives late, and it is the part that cannot be retrofitted cheaply. The terminal is a certified device with its own approval, the kiosk is the host that powers it, presents it and talks to it — and the boundary between those two responsibilities decides the bracket, the cable route and the operating system.

## The short version
Mount the terminal on the cabinet rather than building payment into the cabinet. Cut the bracket for the exact device model, route power and data inside the enclosure, and let the terminal's own certification stay with the terminal. Then choose the operating system by asking which SDK your payment provider supports, not by asking which platform is cheapest.

## Who certifies what
Three different things get called "payment certification" and they belong to different parties:
That division is why a kiosk quote normally excludes the payment device. Where a project does integrate a reader into the cabinet face, the certification scope changes and the schedule usually does too.

## Three ways to connect the terminal
Connection methods used in kiosk projects. The right choice follows from your provider's SDK, not from the cable you prefer.
Method
Typical device
What the kiosk application does
Trade-off
Serial (RS-232) with a vendor protocol
Countertop terminal from Ingenico, Verifone or PAX
Sends the amount and receives the result over a documented protocol; the terminal drives its own UI
Very stable, well understood, but the protocol and cable are device-specific
USB or serial with a provider SDK
Terminal supplied by a PSP with a local SDK
Calls the SDK from the kiosk app; the SDK handles the transaction and the terminal screen
Cleaner integration, but the SDK ties you to one provider and often one OS
Ethernet or cloud (semi-integrated)
Terminal with its own network link
Only displays the amount and polls the result; the terminal talks to the PSP directly
Least coupling and easiest to swap providers, at the cost of a second network drop
Serial is still the most common in unattended kiosks because it survives reboots and needs no driver stack. The provider SDK route is faster to build and harder to leave. The semi-integrated route is the easiest to certify, because the kiosk never handles card data at all.

## The bracket is a drawing, not an accessory
Every terminal has a footprint, a cable exit position, a screen angle and a PIN pad that needs a sight line the next customer cannot share. In practice the mounting drawing fixes four things:
Re-cutting a finished fascia is the single most expensive change in a kiosk project. It is worth waiting a week for the terminal model before releasing the drawing.

## When you need a reader on the kiosk as well
Payment is not the only card interaction. Loyalty cards, staff badges, national ID and access cards are read by the kiosk, not by the payment terminal, and mixing the two confuses customers. The common arrangement is a reader bay on the kiosk for identification, and a separate certified terminal for payment, positioned so the customer does not present the same card twice to two different slots.

## Choosing the operating system
Platform comparison for kiosk applications. Support status refers to the application stack, not to the hardware.
Platform
Best fit
Strengths
Constraints
Windows (IoT Enterprise LTSC)
Applications with a full driver stack, OPOS/JavaPOS peripherals, provider SDKs that ship as Windows libraries

The decision is usually made by one question: does your payment provider ship an SDK for that platform? A platform that cannot talk to the terminal is not a candidate, however good its price. The second question is who maintains the image in the field — remote update tooling differs sharply between the three.

## What to settle before the drawing
- Terminal make, model and mounting drawing, or a decision to use a universal bay
- Connection method and the protocol or SDK version the application will use
- Whether the terminal needs its own network drop or shares the kiosk link
- Operating system, chosen against the SDK list rather than the price list
- Peripheral interfaces: serial, USB or both, and how many of each
- Cash: none, acceptor only, or acceptor with recycler, and the cabinet depth that implies
- Remote update and monitoring tooling, and who operates it
- Key injection and terminal deployment process, owned by the provider

# Why Self-Service Kiosks Fail in 24/7 Operation | Xinyuehong

URL: https://xinyuehongtech.com/news/kiosk-thermal-design-24-7-reliability/

# Why Self-Service Kiosks Fail in 24/7 Operation
By
When a self-service terminal is returned for repair, the fault report usually says "main board dead" or "screen not responding". The root cause underneath is more often the same: heat that had nowhere to go. A kiosk is a sealed sheet-metal box with a computer inside, running at full load in a lobby or on a sidewalk for years without a restart window. Consumer-grade hardware is simply not specified for that duty cycle.
This article walks through where the heat comes from, why it kills electronics, and the design decisions — enclosure, airflow, PC selection — that keep a terminal alive through years of continuous operation.
## Where the heat comes from
A typical kiosk stacks several heat sources into one cabinet:
Individually these are modest loads. The problem is accumulation inside a closed volume: without deliberate airflow, the air inside the cabinet stabilizes 20–35 °C above ambient. In a 35 °C lobby or a sun-facing outdoor bay, the internal air can reach 60–70 °C — beyond the rated limits of most consumer components.
## What heat actually does to the hardware
Electronics do not usually fail instantly from heat; they age. Three mechanisms account for most field failures:
None of these show up in a factory test of a few hours. They appear after 6–24 months of continuous duty, which is exactly when the buyer has stopped paying attention and the operator has started counting downtime.
## Fanless industrial PCs versus consumer mini PCs
The computing platform is where the decision matters most. A consumer mini PC is cheaper on the quote — and more expensive over the contract.
A properly specified
Consumer mini PCs can work in a kiosk
## Enclosure design: giving the heat a path
The cabinet is half of the thermal system. Four rules decide whether it works:
A useful acceptance test during prototyping: run the fully assembled unit at maximum screen brightness with a sustained CPU load for four hours, then measure the air 10 cm above the PC board and the skin temperature above the CPU footprint. Those two numbers predict the machine's service life better than any component datasheet.

- For outdoor: ambient rating with

# Kiosk Touchscreen Technologies Compared | Xinyuehong

URL: https://xinyuehongtech.com/news/kiosk-touchscreen-technology-comparison/

# Kiosk Touchscreen Technologies Compared
By
Most touchscreen comparisons are written for phones and tablets. A self-service kiosk is a different machine: the screen sits behind glass or a bezel, strangers press it all day, cleaning crews spray it, and the enclosure lives outdoors or in a dusty hall. Under those conditions the "best" technology on a spec sheet is often not the best technology behind sheet metal.
This article compares the three touch technologies installed most often — projected capacitive (PCAP), infrared (IR) and surface acoustic wave (SAW) — from the installer's and the operator's point of view.
## How each technology actually senses a touch
The sensing method explains almost every practical difference below.
## Durability against the public
PCAP is the most forgiving against vandalism because the sensor sits behind the cover glass; scratching the surface degrades optics, not touch function. Multi-touch gestures, edge swipes and signature capture all work naturally.
IR frames are exposed at the bezel. They survive hard use well — there is nothing on the glass to wear out — but the optical strip is the vulnerable part: dust, condensation, paint splatter or a jammed flyer can block beams and produce phantom touches. Quality varies a lot between frame suppliers, mainly in how well the firmware filters interference from sunlight and compact-fluorescent lighting.
SAW glass has no overlays and keeps excellent optical clarity, but the wave needs a bare, slightly damp fingertip to absorb energy properly. Hard styluses, thick gloves and dirty screens all degrade accuracy. For public units that get abused, SAW is usually the third choice today.
## Rain, dust, gloves and cleaning chemicals
This is where the technologies separate most clearly:
Condition
PCAP
Infrared
SAW
Rain or condensation on the glass
Needs water-rejection firmware tuning
Beams scatter; phantom touches likely
Drips absorb waves; false inputs
Dusty or greasy film on the glass
Almost unaffected
Beam blocking causes drift over time
Absorption weakens; accuracy drops
Thin disposable gloves
Usually works
Works (beams are broken regardless)
Unreliable
Thick winter gloves
Requires glove-tuned controller
Works
Does not work
Alcohol or ammonia cleaners
Safe through cover glass
Safe for glass; protect the frame seals
Never use harsh solvents on the surface
For outdoor parking, ticketing and border lanes, the default recommendation is PCAP behind chemically strengthened cover glass, with the controller tuned for water rejection. For indoor units in very dusty industrial halls, IR frames with sealed bevels are a proven alternative when multi-touch is not required.
## Optics and enclosure integration
PCAP laminates add layers to the stack, so anti-reflective treatment matters more: without AR coating, sunlight can wash the display out and the controller picks up interference. Budget for the AR or anti-glare cover glass when specifying outdoor PCAP — it is not an option, it is part of the touch system.
IR adds a visible bezel around the display, typically 15–20 mm per side on larger panels. That is why flush-glass designs with narrow borders almost always use PCAP: the IR frame physically does not fit behind 3 mm borders.
SAW offers the cleanest optics of the three — no layers, no bezel — which is why it still appears on indoor directory and information kiosks where hands are clean and vandalism is rare.

## Working on a related kiosk project?
Tell us the installation environment — indoor or outdoor, expected user flow, glove or bare-hand operation — and we will recommend a touch and cover-glass stack that matches it, with reference builds for each combination.

# OEM/ODM Self-Service Kiosk Project Checklist | Xinyuehong

URL: https://xinyuehongtech.com/news/oem-odm-self-service-kiosk-project-checklist/

# OEM/ODM Self-Service Kiosk Project Checklist
By
## Write a brief that gets a real answer
A useful RFQ contains four things: what the unit has to do, what it has to fit into, how many you need and when. Everything else is detail that follows. The failure mode is a one-line email asking for "a custom kiosk price" — the reply can only be a range, and a range is not a budget.
Attach whatever exists: a sketch, a competitor photo, an industrial-design file, a measured drawing of the space. State the screen size you have in mind, the mounting position, the height available and any access constraint. If the unit replaces an existing machine, the dimensions of the old one are the most useful drawing you can send.
## Enclosure: the decisions that change the price
Sheet-metal gauge, finish and sealing are the three cost drivers. A 1.5 mm cold-rolled steel body with a powder coat is the standard reference build; stainless or aluminium changes both material and welding time. A sealed front with a gasketed door adds machining and a sealing test. Colour is cheap when it is a powder-coat batch and expensive when it is a one-off custom match.
Decide early whether the enclosure is a modification of an existing platform or a new design. Modifying an existing cabinet — new cut-outs, a different module stack, a logo — is a fraction of the cost of a new shell, because the tooling, the fold programme and the fit between parts already exist. A new shell means design review, a prototype, fit checks and usually a second iteration.
## Modules and interfaces
List every module with its interface and, where you have a preference, its part number. The kiosk's job is to provide mechanical mounting, power and a data path; the module's vendor provides the driver and the SDK. When a module is chosen late, its dimensions can force a cabinet change, so the module list belongs in the first brief rather than the third revision.
State the power budget too. A unit with a 32-inch bright panel, a receipt printer, an A4 printer and a cash recycler can draw well over 300 W at peak, which changes the power supply, the inlet connector and the heat load the enclosure has to remove.
## Separate branding from engineering
A logo, a colour and a printed panel are branding: they change artwork and a powder-coat batch. A new enclosure, a different cooling path, an added module or a changed screen size are engineering: they change drawings, prototypes and acceptance criteria. Mixing the two in one request makes both the cost and the lead time impossible to estimate, and usually produces a quote that is wrong in one direction or the other.
## Compliance belongs to the market, not the catalogue
State the destination country and the approvals the buyer expects: CE and UKCA in Europe, FCC in the United States, RoHS and REACH for materials, SABER for Saudi Arabia, and accessibility rules such as ADA in the United States or EN 301 549 in Europe. Payment adds its own layer: the terminal is certified by its provider, and the kiosk has to provide a compliant mounting and data path.
Ask for evidence per model rather than a logo on a page. A certificate that names the cabinet and the module list is worth more than a badge, and a supplier who cannot produce one is telling you something useful.
## Samples, acceptance and change control
Agree what "accepted" means before the first unit is built: which tests, on which modules, with what pass criteria. A practical set is a 12-hour burn-in at ambient, a full transaction run on every module, a print quality check, a touch calibration check and a visual inspection against the drawing. Record the result and sign it off — that document is the baseline for every later change.
Change control is the other half. After sign-off, every request should be classified as cosmetic, functional or structural, with the cost and schedule impact stated before work starts. Projects that skip this step discover the cost of a late module change after the cabinets are already cut.
## Timeline and milestones
A modification of an existing platform typically runs: brief and drawing review, sample build, sample approval, first batch, inspection, shipment. A new enclosure adds a design iteration and a fit-check prototype. Ask each supplier to commit to milestone dates rather than a single lead-time figure, so a slip is visible while there is still time to react.

# How Much Does a Self-Service Kiosk Cost? 2026 Price Guide

URL: https://xinyuehongtech.com/news/self-service-kiosk-cost/


# How Much Does a Self-Service Kiosk Cost?
By
Kiosk prices are quoted per build, not per category. The same 27-inch cabinet can leave the factory at US$900 or US$2,400 depending on which readers, printer, panel and computing platform are inside it. The ranges below are reference points for 2026, FOB Shenzhen, for orders from one unit to about 100 units.

Two assumptions sit behind those numbers: standard module set (no new tooling) and payment by bank transfer. Freight, import duty, market certification and software are quoted separately, because none of them belong to the cabinet.

## What is inside the price
A quotation is a bill of materials with margin on top. In a typical kiosk build the split looks like this. Percentages are shares of the unit price, not of the cost.
Indicative cost structure for a floor-standing kiosk with readers and a printer.
Line

What moves it

## The five things that move the price most

### 1. Screen size, panel grade and brightness
A 15.6-inch industrial panel and a 32-inch 2560 × 1440 panel are not the same purchase. Moving from a 21.5-inch 1080p panel to a 32-inch QHD panel typically adds US$250–500 to the bill of materials before any mechanical changes. High-brightness panels for outdoor or window-facing units add more again.

### 2. Touch technology
Projected capacitive (PCAP) is the default for indoor public terminals. Infrared touch is cheaper on large sizes but adds bezel depth and is more sensitive to dust. Resistive survives gloves and wet hands but feels dated. The gap between the cheapest and the most durable stack on the same screen is usually US$60–200.

### 3. Card readers, PIN pads and payment devices
This is where quotations diverge most. A contactless-only reader is inexpensive; a full set of chip, swipe and contactless plus a certified encrypting PIN pad can add several hundred dollars. Where the acquirer requires a specific certified payment terminal, that device is usually bought separately and mounted on the kiosk rather than integrated into it.

### 4. The computing platform
An Android board, an Intel Celeron fanless box and a Core i5 box with 16 GB of RAM sit in different price bands. The right question is not which is cheapest but which one your software, drivers and payment SDK actually run on. Replacing a platform after the enclosure is drawn costs far more than choosing the correct one at the start.

### 5. Order size, tooling and lead time
At one unit you pay for setup. At 100 units the same cabinet may drop 15–25%, mostly because laser programming, fixtures and powder-coat batches are amortised. New tooling for a custom enclosure is a one-off cost, typically US$2,000–8,000 depending on complexity, and it does not disappear at higher volumes. Rush orders add cost at the component level, not the assembly level.

## Costs that are not on the quotation
Buyers comparing two kiosk quotes often compare the wrong totals. These lines are usually missing from both:

## How to compare two quotations
Ask both suppliers for the same eleven lines. If a quote cannot answer them, it is not comparable, however low the total looks.
Line-by-line comparison list for kiosk quotations.
Item
What to ask for
Enclosure
Steel thickness, finish, service-door design
Panel
Brand, brightness in nits, resolution, backlight life
Touch
Technology, cover glass, number of touch points
Computer
CPU model, RAM, storage, operating system image
Printer
Brand, paper width, cutter rating, duty cycle
Readers
Exact model numbers, interfaces, certification status
Test report
Burn-in duration, what was exercised, who signs it off
Certification
Which marks are included, and who pays for testing
Warranty
Length, what is covered, who pays return freight
Lead time
From deposit or drawing approval, not from enquiry
Packing
Crate type, pallet dimensions, container loading plan

## The cheapest way to start
Most first projects do not need a new enclosure. They need a working terminal in front of real users, fast. A practical low-cost route:
- Order one prototype unit from a standard cabinet and standard module set — minimum order quantity of one is common in this industry.
- Skip custom tooling in round one. Prove the flow first; tool the enclosure once the service is validated.
- Use a certified third-party payment terminal instead of an integrated payment module. It is cheaper to certify and easier to swap.
- Run the pilot for four to six weeks and measure transactions per unit per day, not satisfaction scores.
- Scale with a production batch that shares the pilot's enclosure, so the drawings, fixtures and test procedure are reused.

# Self-Service Kiosk Modules: What to Specify | Xinyuehong

URL: https://xinyuehongtech.com/news/self-service-kiosk-modules-guide/

# Self-Service Kiosk Modules: What to Specify
By
A kiosk quotation is mostly a list of modules. Two units can look identical from the outside and differ by a factor of three in cost, simply because one carries a certified card reader and a cash recycler while the other only needs a QR scanner and a receipt printer. Knowing what each module does — and what it obliges you to maintain — is the fastest way to keep a project inside budget.
## The eight module families
The table below is the map for the rest of this guide. Use it as a checklist when you write an RFQ: mark each family as required, optional or not applicable before you ask anyone for a price.
Module families used in self-service terminals
Family
What does the work a customer cannot do on a screen
Typical options
Contact IC, contactless RFID, magnetic stripe, national ID, passport MRZ, 1D/2D imager, thermal or A4 printer, PIN pad, bill acceptor, coin hopper, cash recycler, camera, fingerprint, NFC
Chosen by
The transaction: what the customer must present, prove, pay with, or take away
Watch out for
Driver support on your operating system, power budget, service access, certification in the destination market
## 1. Card and identity reading
This is the family most projects underestimate, because "card reader" covers six different devices. A contact IC reader handles bank and CPU cards inserted into a slot. A contactless RFID reader (13.56 MHz, ISO 14443 A/B, MIFARE) handles tap cards, staff badges and transport cards. A magnetic stripe reader handles older bank and membership cards. An ID reader at 125 kHz handles proximity cards used for building access. A national ID reader reads the chip on a resident identity card, which is mandatory for hospital, telecom and government self-service in several markets. A passport MRZ scanner reads the two-line code at the bottom of a passport page for border, hotel and immigration counters.
The practical constraint is never whether the reader exists — it is whether it has a driver for the operating system you intend to run, and whether its certification is valid in the country where the unit will be installed. Confirm both in writing before the cabinet is tooled.
## 2. Barcode and QR scanning
A 1D laser engine reads printed linear barcodes: tickets, printed vouchers, product labels. A 2D imager reads both linear codes and matrix codes, and it is the only option if customers will present a QR code on a phone screen — mobile wallet payment, e-tickets, loyalty codes, health codes. Because phone screens are backlit and often cracked or dimmed, a 2D engine needs adequate illumination and a scan window angled so the screen faces the imager rather than the ceiling.
Two mounting styles dominate. A presentation window behind tempered glass — the scan deck — is the robust choice for public counters because there is no protruding hardware to break. A flush-mounted engine in the bezel saves space on wall-mounted and countertop units. Both are read by the same 2D engine; the difference is how much abuse the installation will take.
## 3. Printing
An 80 mm thermal receipt printer with an auto-cutter is the default for payment, queue tickets and transaction records; 58 mm is used where the receipt is short and paper cost matters. An A4 laser printer is specified when the customer must leave with a document — a medical record, a statement, a certificate, a boarding pass on paper. Parking and cinema installations often use a dedicated ticket printer with a larger roll and a different media path.
Specify three things that are easy to forget: roll capacity, whether the printer loads from the front or the rear, and whether a paper-near-end sensor is wired to the management software. In the field, a kiosk that runs out of paper without warning is a kiosk that is out of service.
## 4. Computing platform and operating system
Two platform families cover most builds. Android boards such as the RK3568 and RK3399, with 2–8 GB of RAM and 16–64 GB of eMMC storage, suit single-purpose applications, digital signage hybrids and cost-sensitive deployments. Windows and Linux builds on Intel Celeron J6412, optionally Core i3 or i5, with 4–16 GB of DDR memory and 64–512 GB of SSD storage, suit legacy peripherals, heavy browser applications and anything that needs a specific Windows driver.
Choose the platform last, not first. It is a consequence of the modules you selected: if the ID reader only has a Windows driver, the platform decision has already been made for you. Request kiosk-mode lock-down, a hardware watchdog and remote device management, so the unit recovers from a frozen application without a site visit.
## 5. Display and touch
Sizes run from 15.6-inch countertop panels to 32-inch floor-standing displays. A 32-inch portrait panel at 2560 × 1440 gives enough vertical space for a full registration form plus a guidance column, which is why it has become the reference size for multi-step workflows. Smaller panels at 1920 × 1080 remain the right choice for wall-mounted and desktop units.
Touch is projected capacitive (PCAP) with ten points in nearly all current designs, under tempered or anti-glare glass. Where a PIN is entered, ask for a privacy filter. Where the screen faces a window, ask for higher brightness and optical bonding. A second display mounted above the main screen costs little and is used for queue guidance, advertising or showing the operator's side of the transaction on dual-screen counters.
## 6. Payment and cash handling
Card payment splits into three approaches. A card reader integrated into the cabinet handles the card and sends the transaction to a payment gateway. A certified PIN pad handles the encrypted PIN entry, which is what banks and most regulated markets require. A bracket for an external POS terminal lets the acquirer supply and certify their own device — slower to integrate, but it removes certification risk from the kiosk builder.
QR payment is cheaper than card payment because it can work by displaying a code for the customer to scan, or by scanning the code the customer shows. Cash handling is the most expensive family: a bill acceptor, a coin hopper and a cash recycler each add weight, a reconciliation routine, a cash collection schedule and a service contract. Model the cost of cash collection before you specify it.
## 7. Cameras and biometrics
A camera above the display serves face capture for KYC, membership enrolment, access control and anti-fraud records. A fingerprint module serves the same purposes where a fingerprint is the established credential. Both raise data questions before they raise technical ones: where images are stored, how long they are retained, and which regulation applies. Settle that with your compliance owner before the module is ordered.
## 8. Enclosure, power and connectivity
The cabinet is a module too. A floor-standing base with lockable castors lets one unit be moved for cleaning and repositioned between seasons; a fixed base is more stable and slightly cheaper. Countertop and wall-mounted cabinets serve the same applications where floor space is scarce. Powder-coated steel is the default; a higher ingress rating, sealed cable entries and a filtered ventilation path are required for semi-outdoor and industrial sites.
Power and network planning belongs in the same conversation: Ethernet as primary, Wi-Fi or 4G where cabling is impractical, and a small UPS so a power cut produces a graceful shutdown and a completed transaction record rather than a corrupted database.
## Module sets by scenario
The table below shows the sets we most often build. Treat it as a starting point: these are the combinations that survive contact with real queues.

## Five questions to settle before you order
## What to send with your module RFQ
An RFQ that lists modules with interfaces and quantities gets a comparable quotation; one that says "kiosk with card reader" does not. Include the target operating system, the module list with preferred interface (USB, RS232, TTL), the daily transaction volume, the installation environment, the certification markets, the expected service access and the quantity at first order and at full rollout.
## Working on a module list right now?
Send the workflow you need and the modules you think you need, and we will reply with the ones that are missing, the ones that are redundant, and the driver constraints we can see.

# Self-Service Kiosks for Saudi Arabia | Xinyuehong

URL: https://xinyuehongtech.com/saudi-arabia/


# Self-Service Kiosks for Saudi Arabia
Kiosk hardware supplied into Saudi projects, with the parts that usually get missed planned in: SABER conformity, Arabic interface and receipt printing, 230 V / 60 Hz power and sea freight to Jeddah or Dammam.

## What changes when the kiosk ships to Saudi Arabia
A kiosk built for a European hospital and one built for a Riyadh service centre can use the same cabinet and the same reader stack. What changes is the compliance file, the interface language, the printing and the power. Those four items decide whether the unit clears customs and whether staff can use it on day one.
The conformity route is the one buyers underestimate. Electrical products entering Saudi Arabia go through the SABER platform: a Product Certificate of Conformity is issued for the model, and a Shipment Certificate is issued per consignment. Both are tied to the importer of record, not to the factory. A quotation that does not mention this is not a complete quotation.
Arabic is not a translation task. The interface runs right-to-left, which changes the layout of forms and the position of navigation, and the receipt printer has to carry an Arabic code page in its firmware. A terminal that prints a mangled receipt in Arabic will be switched off by the counter staff within a week.
Finally, the power. Saudi Arabia runs 230 V at 60 Hz, and socket types vary between buildings, so the build is specified with the plug and the input range agreed in writing rather than with a default European cord.

## Six points to settle before the drawing

### SABER, not just CE
A CE file helps the laboratory work, but entry needs the Saudi Product Certificate and a shipment certificate per consignment. Confirm who holds the importer of record before production starts.

### Arabic first, RTL
Interface strings, form direction and number formatting all change. The screen size and the font size have to be re-checked with Arabic text, which is taller than Latin at the same point size.

### Arabic code page
Thermal printers need firmware support for the Arabic character set. Ask for a printed sample in Arabic before the batch runs, not after.

### 230 V / 60 Hz
Socket type varies by building. The build is specified with the plug type, the input range and the surge protection agreed in writing.

### mada-certified devices
Card acceptance goes through a certified payment terminal, normally provided by the acquirer. The kiosk supplies mounting, power and the cable route rather than an integrated payment module.

### Heat and dust
Indoor malls are cool; service halls, industrial sites and covered outdoor positions are not. Ambient temperature, dust and direct sun decide the fanless platform and the panel brightness.

## Where these terminals are used in the Kingdom

## Models that fit Saudi projects
Reference units from our range. Every configuration is confirmed in writing per project.
23.8-inch working screen with a 21.5-inch Arabic guidance screen above it, multi-slot national ID, social-security and bank card reader bank.

## From order to customs clearance
Budget the conformity work as a project cost rather than a per-unit cost: it is paid once per model family, and it is the line most often missing when buyers compare a Chinese quote with a local distributor's price. The
